newsitem.title: ALBANIA: IMF discusses resuming support for Albania.
newsitem.headline: IMF discusses resuming support for Albania.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund is in contact with Albania's government in waiting and is ready to send a negotiating mission next month if the security situation allows, diplomats and economists said on Tuesday.
Final results of the June 29 parliamentary elections and the run-offs that followed have not yet been announced but the broad outlines of Socialist leader Fatos Nano's government are already known.
Interim finance minister Arben Malaj is expected to retain his post, while current prime minister Bashkim Fino is likely to stay on as deputy premier.

One of the first tasks of the new government will be to approve a decree enabling international auditors to come in and wind up remaining high-interest investment schemes. The collapse of five pyramid schemes led to violent protests earlier this year.
"The international financial institutions have made it very clear that they won't resume lending until the remaining schemes are closed," said a Western diplomat.
The IMF suspended support for Albania in 1995, but its return is a precondition for other bilateral and multilateral lending.

"They (the IMF) are waiting for the new government to be formed and for parliament to convene," the diplomat said. Parliament is expected to meet by early next week, and the sources said the IMF could then send a mission in August.
Western countries are keen to offer technical and financial help to avert a new influx of refugees to nearby Italy and Greece.
Rome will host a high-level international conference on Albania in late July to assess the post-election situation and discuss further economic and financial aid.
Albania has chrome and copper deposits, potential for a tourist industry capitalising on its historic sites and Adriatic beaches, and a skilled workforce.
But the limited banking system and lack of legal reforms, as well as the security situation, are likely to deter foreign investors in the short term.
A 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew remains in force and the new government will face the problem of controlling an estimated one million looted weapons now in private hands.
The Socialist Party, which will have a more than two-thirds majority in the new parliament, has promised to compensate pyramid investors as much as possible, and to ensure transparency.
Economists and diplomats say financial support will have to be carefully monitored to ensure it is used for the intended purpose.
